papers.title: Novel sleep scoring method for neurodegenerative diseases: feasibility and reliability in advanced Parkinson disease.
papers.abstract: In neurodegenerative diseases, damage to sleep-wake regulating brain regions alters sleep architecture (e.g., loss of spindles and K-complexes, EEG slowing during wakefulness and REM sleep), challenging the current American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) rules for scoring sleep. In Parkinson disease (PD) patients, we assessed the feasibility and interrater reliability of a previously described novel sleep scoring methodology. Video-polysomnography of 15 PD patients and five age-matched controls were scored blinded by five trained raters (two neurologists and three technicians) with different levels of expertise. Recordings were first scored empirically following the AASM methodology and, when necessary, scored again using the following additional abnormal stages: abnormal Wake, Subwake, Undifferentiated NREM (UNREM) sleep, Poorly Structured N2 sleep, and abnormal REM sleep. Sleep microstructure alterations (e.g., encapsulated REM sleep behavior disorder) were also evaluated. The novel scoring method showed substantial interrater agreement (kappa = 0.75), comparable to the AASM method (kappa = 0.73). UNREM sleep was identified in 12 patients, Subwake in nine, and abnormal Wake, encapsulated REM sleep behavior disorder and abnormal REM sleep in seven. No abnormal stages were observed in three early PD patients or in any control. The presence of the abnormal sleep stages was associated with ageing and advanced PD with cognitive impairment and motor fluctuations. The novel sleep scoring methodology, which includes abnormal wakefulness as well as NREM and REM sleep stages, is feasible, reliable, and applicable in clinical practice for advanced PD patients undergoing video-polysomnography.

ai.reason: Proposes alternative sleep-stage labels for abnormal EEG architecture, highly relevant to generalizable/transferable sleep staging and vigilance-state classification methods.
ai.summary: The authors tested a novel sleep scoring methodology incorporating abnormal Wake, Subwake, Undifferentiated NREM, Poorly Structured N2, and abnormal REM stages in 15 advanced Parkinson disease patients and five controls, scored blinded by five raters. The method showed substantial interrater agreement (kappa = 0.75), comparable to AASM scoring (kappa = 0.73), and abnormal stages were associated with ageing and advanced PD with cognitive impairment and motor fluctuations.

papers.title: Longitudinal persistence of EEG brain fingerprints: phase and complex coherency geometry across sessions and functional states
papers.abstract: Sensor-level EEG coherency can distinguish individuals, although its phase and magnitude patterns may reflect neural activity, source mixing, and recording geometry. We evaluated two geometric representations of complex coherency - unit phasors and full complex coherency - alongside triangle holonomies and magnitude-only descriptors. Using direct enrollment-probe matching without a trained identity classifier, we analyzed three independent longitudinal cohorts: RestCog (N = 60; approximately one month), L-FAME (N = 44; six weeks), and Dortmund (N = 206; approximately five years). In eyes-closed rest-to-rest matching, alpha phasors identified 81.67% of participants in RestCog (AUC 0.9473) and 79.55% in L-FAME (AUC 0.9735); full complex coherency identified 78.33% and 84.09%, respectively. After five years in Dortmund, fixed row-standardized alpha-beta fusion yielded 77.67% rank-1 identification (AUC 0.9744) for phasors and 70.39% (AUC 0.9527) for full coherency. Changes in functional state exposed different strengths: full coherency preserved higher rank-1 accuracy in some monthly RestCog rest-to-task comparisons, whereas alpha phasors retained higher verification AUC. Switching between eyes-closed and eyes-open recordings in Dortmund substantially weakened identification with both representations. Triangle holonomies also retained individual information across visits. An exact factorization of complex cosine shows how magnitude-pattern alignment and magnitude-weighted phase agreement contribute to full-coherency matching. Together, the results establish longitudinally discriminative structure in measured scalp EEG coherency over weeks to years, while distinguishing persistence across visits from robustness to changes in recording state.

ai.reason: Longitudinal phase/complex-coherency geometry across sessions and states supports interpretable connectivity features and longitudinal modeling, directly relevant to spectral and state-space interests.
ai.summary: Investigated the longitudinal persistence of EEG connectivity-based individual fingerprints using phase and complex coherency geometry across three cohorts spanning one month to five years, without a trained identity classifier. Alpha phasors identified 81.67% (RestCog) and 79.55% (L-FAME) of participants in rest-to-rest matching, and after five years 77.67% rank-1 identification was retained, while state changes (eyes-open/closed, task) weakened identification, distinguishing temporal persistence from robustness across functional states.

papers.title: Sleep Renormalizes Negative Emotional Generalization
papers.abstract: Overgeneralization of negative experiences co-occurs with sleep disruption and characterizes anxiety and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). A strategically-designed behavioral paradigm tested whether sleep shifts emotional generalization away from negative and toward positive representations. Participants learned positive, negative, or neutral face-outcome associations, then completed immediate and delayed generalization testing with morphed faces after sleep or wakefulness. Sleep selectively enhanced positive generalization, whereas wakefulness favored negative generalization. To uncover the underlying neural mechanisms, individual variability in generalization was examined using fMRI and high-density EEG. Amygdala and limbic activity during outcome-processing predicted both stronger immediate negative generalization and a sleep-specific shift toward positive generalization. Additionally, sleep-spindle activity positively correlated with post-sleep increases in positive generalization and reductions in negative generalization. Together, these findings identify a neural mechanism through which sleep reduces negative bias while strengthening positive representations, highlighting a pathway by which sleep may protect against maladaptive generalization associated with anxiety and PTSD.

ai.reason: Sleep-spindle EEG analysis in a sleep-manipulation paradigm is relevant mechanistic background, though not a computational-method contribution.
ai.summary: Using a face-outcome generalization paradigm combined with fMRI and high-density EEG, the authors report that sleep selectively enhanced positive generalization while wakefulness favored negative generalization. Amygdala/limbic outcome-processing activity predicted a sleep-specific shift toward positive generalization, and sleep-spindle activity correlated with increased positive and reduced negative generalization.

papers.title: Autonomic Reactivity and EEG-defined Clusters Reveal Distinct Chronic Pain Profiles.
papers.abstract: This study examined whether integrating stress-related heart rate variability (HRV) with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) could characterize physiological subgroups in Chronic pain after spine surgery (CPSS). A total of 177 patients completed pain- and emotion-related questionnaires, a 3-minute resting-state EEG recording, and HRV assessments during baseline, mental arithmetic stress, and recovery. Participants were grouped by the direction of stress-related low-frequency/high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio change. Principal component analysis and unsupervised clustering were applied to 437 EEG features encompassing absolute power, cerebral asymmetry, and theta/beta ratio (TBR). After multivariate outlier detection, 168 participants underwent clustering. A 2 × 2 factorial ANOVA examined HRV-group and EEG-cluster effects on pain scores. LF/HF -decreased group (n = 56) reported higher depressive symptom scores than the increase group (n = 121, P = 0.045), without significant pain differences. Among 437 EEG features, PC1 reflected beta activity (34.39% variance), PC2 frontal/frontotemporal asymmetry (14.52%), and PC3 TBR features (9.55%). Two EEG clusters (n = 88 and n = 80) showed no significant pain- or emotion-related differences. Factorial analysis revealed nonsignificant HRV (P = .056) and EEG main effects (P = .107), but a nominally significant interaction [P = .030, partial η² = .028 (HC3-robust P = .044)]. Within EEG Cluster 0, the LF/HF-decrease group reported higher pain scores than the LF/HF-increase group (70.9 vs. 42.3; Tukey-adjusted P = .019). Integrating HRV-EEG profiles may help characterize CPSS heterogeneity. These exploratory findings, without study-wide multiplicity adjustment, require independent validation before clinical application.

ai.reason: Feature-based unsupervised clustering of resting EEG with interpretable spectral features is somewhat transferable, but the chronic pain application limits direct relevance.
ai.summary: In 177 patients with chronic pain after spine surgery, the authors integrated stress-related HRV LF/HF changes with resting-state EEG features via PCA and unsupervised clustering. A nominally significant HRV-group by EEG-cluster interaction was found, with the LF/HF-decrease group reporting higher pain scores within one EEG cluster, though main effects were not significant and findings require validation.

papers.title: Eyes-open resting-state EEG microstate analysis using ratio-normalized parameters across four- and seven-class solutions in healthy controls, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: BackgroundResting-state EEG microstate analysis indexes large-scale network dynamics, yet the value of ratio-normalized temporal parameters under the eyes-open resting (EOR) condition remains unexplored across the cognitive decline continuum.ObjectiveTo examine whether ratio-normalized microstate parameters from four- and seven-class clustering solutions under EOR differentiate healthy controls (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD).MethodsOne hundred and eighty participants (HC, MCI, and AD; n = 60 each) were recruited from a hospital-based cohort in an elderly Korean population. Resting-state EEG recorded under EOR was analyzed using MICROSTATELAB in EEGLAB. Absolute temporal parameters (duration, occurrence, coverage) and ratio-normalized forms (relative duration, relative occurrence) were compared using ANCOVA with age as covariate, false discovery rate (FDR) correction, and Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons.ResultsIn the four-class solution, three parameters reached nominal significance, none surviving FDR correction across the full set of 20 tests: coverage of Microstate B (visual network; F(2176) = 3.561, p = 0.030), relative occurrence of Microstate B (F(2176) = 5.281, p = 0.006), and relative occurrence of Microstate E (executive network; F(2176) = 3.816, p = 0.024). MCI showed higher visual and lower executive microstate engagement than AD (p ≤ 0.023); no contrast involving HC was significant. Absolute occurrence parameters were non-significant whereas their ratio-normalized counterparts were significant. The seven-class solution yielded no corrected effects.ConclusionsRatio-normalized EOR microstate parameters distinguished MCI from AD through visual and executive network engagement, with small-to-moderate effects and HC intermediate. The four-class solution outperformed the seven-class solution, contrasting with eyes-closed reports. As these analyses were exploratory and did not survive correction, confirmation in independent cohorts is required.

ai.reason: Microstate analysis with ratio-normalized features and EEGLAB tooling is adjacent; normalization idea is mildly relevant but clinical MCI/AD focus and null results reduce value.
ai.summary: In 180 participants (60 each HC, MCI, AD), ratio-normalized eyes-open resting-state EEG microstate parameters from four- and seven-class solutions were compared. The four-class solution showed nominal MCI-versus-AD differences in visual (Microstate B) and executive (Microstate E) network engagement, but no effects survived FDR correction and the seven-class solution yielded none.

papers.title: Increased variability in visual processing in children with autism
papers.abstract: The visual evoked potential (VEP) indexes sensory processing, but the neurophysiological basis of altered VEP amplitudes in autism remains unclear. We examined whether reduced VEP amplitude reflects increased trial-to-trial neural variability and whether this variability relates to electrophysiological markers of cortical excitation/inhibition and developmental functioning. Pattern-reversal VEPs were analyzed in 102 typically developing (TD; 44 female) and 105 autistic (AUT; 15 female) children aged 2-12 years. N1 and N1-P1 amplitudes and inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) were computed. Resting-state periodic alpha activity and aperiodic exponent were derived using spectral parameterization. Associations among VEP, resting EEG, age, and developmental/behavioral measures were assessed using multiple linear regression. AUT children exhibited reduced N1 amplitude and lower ITPC, with marginally reduced N1-P1 amplitude. Higher ITPC was strongly associated with larger N1 and N1-P1 amplitudes, and group differences in VEP amplitudes were no longer significant after accounting for ITPC. Greater periodic alpha activity was associated with higher ITPC and larger N1-P1 amplitude, while a steeper aperiodic exponent was associated with higher ITPC in the pooled cohort. Within AUT children, higher ITPC was associated with better nonverbal development, verbal cognition, and language scores. Reduced VEP amplitudes in autism may primarily reflect increased trial-to-trial variability rather than systematically weaker stimulus-evoked responses. Associations between ITPC and resting EEG measures suggest that cortical excitation/inhibition may contribute to sensory response reliability. These findings identify neural response consistency as a developmentally relevant feature of visual processing in autism.

ai.reason: Trial-to-trial phase coherence and spectral parameterization are relevant analytical tools, but the pediatric VEP/autism focus is adjacent rather than core.
ai.summary: Analyzed pattern-reversal VEPs in 102 typically developing and 105 autistic children aged 2-12, showing reduced N1 amplitude and lower inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) in autism; group VEP amplitude differences vanished after accounting for ITPC. Higher ITPC was linked to resting alpha activity and, within autistic children, to better nonverbal, verbal, and language scores.

papers.title: A Retrospective Real-World Assessment of Motor Status After Stroke Using a Home-Based Brain-Computer Interface
papers.abstract: Background: Upper extremity impairment persists in many stroke survivors, and few treatments are effective for severe chronic deficits. Brain-computer interface (BCI) therapy, which pairs decoded motor-intention-associated electrophysiology with sensory feedback, has improved upper extremity impairment in randomized trials, including in patients with severe paresis. Whether these benefits translate to routine care has rarely been evaluated. This study examined upper extremity motor recovery through 1 year among patients prescribed at-home BCI therapy in clinical practice. Methods: This retrospective observational study included adults who were prescribed the IpsiHand System, an electroencephalography-based BCI, through a commercial US home therapy program, had a baseline Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) assessment, and averaged >1 session per week through their last assessment. Occupational therapists administered the UEFM by video every 4 weeks. The primary outcome was UEFM change from baseline to week 12. A mixed model for repeated measures estimated change through week 52, with multiple imputation sensitivity analyses for missing data. Results: Of 452 patients included in analyses (mean time since stroke, 5.4 +/- 5.4 years), mean baseline UEFM was 20.1 +/- 14.6, with 333 patients (73.7%) having severe motor impairment (UEFM 0-28). At week 12, mean UEFM change was 4.3 points (95% CI, 3.7-4.9; P<0.001), and 31.7% achieved the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 5.25 points. Mean change reached the MCID at week 16 (5.6, 95% CI [4.8, 6.4]). Model-estimated change in UEFM continued to improve through 1 year, being 6.1 (95% CI, 5.5-6.8) at week 24 and 8.1 (95% CI, 6.8-9.4) at week 52. Conclusions: Among regular users of at-home BCI therapy in routine care, most of whom had severe chronic impairment, UEFM scores improved by 12 weeks, reached MCID by 16 weeks, and continued to increase through 1 year. At-home BCI therapy merits evaluation in randomized trials with follow-up beyond 12 weeks.

ai.reason: At-home EEG BCI with longitudinal outcomes is adjacent, but the clinical rehabilitation endpoint rather than signal-processing method limits relevance.
ai.summary: Retrospective observational study of 452 stroke survivors (mean 5.4 years post-stroke, 73.7% severe impairment) using at-home EEG-based BCI (IpsiHand) therapy, with UEFM improving 4.3 points at week 12, reaching the MCID (~5.6 points) by week 16, and rising to 8.1 points at week 52.

papers.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models
papers.abstract: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

ai.reason: Human iEEG study of oscillatory predictive routing; spectral power analysis methods are adjacent and transferable, but the contribution is cognitive neuroscience rather than tooling.
ai.summary: Using human intracranial EEG from seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm, the study tested predictive routing predictions by measuring theta, alpha-beta and high-gamma power during auditory deviance, multisensory integration and McGurk incongruence. Superior temporal cortex showed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power for auditory deviance and McGurk stimuli, whereas frontal areas showed the alpha-beta decrease without a high-gamma prediction error signal and instead a strong theta-band prediction error in the McGurk condition.

papers.title: High-frequency EEG activity moderates the association between amyloid burden and tau in cognitively normal adults
papers.abstract: Background: Resting electroencephalogram (EEG) may capture early excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) imbalance in Alzheimer's disease, but its relationship to beta-amyloid and tau in cognitively normal adults is unclear. Methods: We analyzed resting-state EEG from 24 older adults, 21 cognitively normal (13 beta-amyloid-negative, 8 beta-amyloid-positive) and 3 with MCI/AD (all beta-amyloid-positive), with beta-amyloid positron emission tomography (PET); 20 of the cognitively normal adults also had tau PET. Four parietal measures related to E-I balance and excitability (periodic gamma power, alpha-gamma and theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling [PAC], and the aperiodic exponent) were related to beta-amyloid burden and to early medial temporal lobe (MTL) tau, adjusting for age and sex. Results: In 21 cognitively normal adults, higher beta-amyloid burden was associated with higher parietal periodic gamma power (beta= +0.50, p = 0.025). No E-I measure was associated with MTL tau across all participants. However, in beta-amyloid-positive adults, higher periodic gamma was associated with higher MTL tau, most strongly in the entorhinal cortex (beta = +0.90, p = 0.002), with no association in beta-amyloid-negative adults. Importantly, periodic gamma also moderated the association between beta-amyloid and MTL tau (p = 0.012; consistent across MTL regions after FDR correction). Conclusions: In this pilot study, parietal periodic gamma, an EEG marker of cortical excitability, increased with beta-amyloid burden and was related to MTL tau only in the presence of beta-amyloid. Periodic gamma is a candidate marker of beta-amyloid-related E-I imbalance that warrants confirmation in larger samples.

papers.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
papers.abstract: Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.

papers.title: A multimodal dataset of EEG, eye-tracking, and physiological signals during naturalistic smartphone interactions
papers.abstract: Smartphones have become pervasive tools for communication, information consumption, and digital interaction, yet the neurophysiological dynamics associated with naturalistic smartphone use remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we present a multimodal physiological dataset collected during ecologically valid smartphone interaction and a subsequent relaxation condition. Twenty-three participants engaged with their most frequently used smartphone application (primarily gaming or short form video) for ten minutes, followed by a five-minute passive viewing of a standardized nature video. Simultaneous recordings were obtained from electroencephalography (EEG; 64 channels), wearable eye-tracking, photoplethysmography (PPG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors. Questionnaire-based assessments, including the smartphone addiction scale (SAS) and the mobile phone problematic use scale (MPPUS), are also collected to characterize individual differences in smartphone-related behavioral traits. All data streams are synchronized using transistor-transistor logic (TTL) trigger signals to ensure precise temporal alignment across modalities. The dataset is organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification and is publicly available on OpenNeuro (Accession Number: ds007537). This dataset enables the investigation of neural, ocular, and autonomic responses during smartphone interaction and supports multimodal analysis of diverse smartphone behaviors while preserving ecological validity.

papers.title: Diagnostic value of extending outpatient EEG to record sleep - A retrospective study.
papers.abstract: Evidence for the utility of sleep electroencephalography (EEG) in the diagnosis of epilepsy is inconsistent, often necessitating repeat visits and sleep deprivation (SD), which increases patient and resource burden. In our setting in India, patients are often referred for EEG immediately following consultation (single visit) and EEG sessions are extended to allow for spontaneous sleep acquisition without prior SD. We aimed to evaluate the success rate of achieving sleep during these extended outpatient recordings and its incremental diagnostic yield for interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs). We retrospectively analyzed 1762 outpatient EEGs from patients (45% female) with suspected or known epilepsy. All patients underwent an extended routine EEG (~40-50 min), incorporating standard activation procedures and aiming to capture spontaneous sleep where possible. Successful sleep acquisition was defined as the attainment of at least NREM stage N2. IED detection rates were compared between wakefulness and sleep across different epilepsy types. Sleep was achieved in 70.5% of patients (median age, 28 years; IQR: 16-55; range, 0.3-90). The proportion attaining sleep increased with recording duration, from 36.7% at 20 min to 55.6% at 30 min and 66.7% at 50 min, with a median time to sleep onset of 20 min. Among 1199 patients with both awake and sleep states captured, wakefulness identified IEDs in 29% (n = 350), while sleep captured unique IEDs in an additional 12% (n = 141), increasing the total yield significantly. In a sub-analysis of confirmed epilepsy cases (n = 751), wakefulness showed IEDs in 42% (n = 315), with sleep adding another 16% (n = 123). The diagnostic yield of sleep recordings was significantly higher than that of wakefulness alone (OR: 1.31; 95% CI: 1.02-1.68; p = 0.043), particularly among adults with idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) (OR: 2.20; 95% CI: 1.30-3.73; p = 0.004) and children with self-limited epilepsy (OR: ∞; p = 0.031). Despite a busy outpatient setting, 70.5% of patients attained N2 sleep during an extended EEG recording without SD. Sleep capture increased progressively with recording duration, with the greatest incremental gain between 20 and 30 min, suggesting that a modest extension beyond 20 min substantially increases the likelihood of capturing sleep. Sleep recording increased IED detection over wakefulness alone, particularly in children, in adults with IGE, and in self-limited epilepsies. Whether this approach can substitute for a sleep-deprived EEG requires prospective, head-to-head evaluation.

papers.title: Machine Learning Classification of Bipolar Disorder Across Mood States Using Natural Language Processing and Speech Analysis: Observational Study.
papers.abstract: Bipolar disorder (BP) affects 1% to 3% of adults worldwide, with diagnostic delays averaging 6 years and high initial misdiagnosis rates. The absence of objective diagnostic measures contributes to clinical uncertainty and suboptimal outcomes. This study aimed to (1) develop a machine learning model for BP diagnosis and mood state classification using linguistic and acoustic features, (2) identify features associated with different mood states by comparing each with healthy controls (HC), and (3) explore whether features distinguish between mood states within BP. We analyzed data prospectively collected over 7 years from 61 patients with BP and 99 HC across Japan. Speech samples were collected via semistructured interviews over 1 to 5 visits and analyzed cross-sectionally, using aggregated or single-visit observations per participant rather than within-person longitudinal modeling. We extracted 6373 acoustic features (openSMILE 3.0, ComParE 2016) and 211 linguistic features. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-regularized logistic regression with nested cross-validation and age- and sex-matched undersampling was used. Mood states were classified as depressive state (DS; Hamilton Depression Rating Scale-17 [HAMD-17] ≥8, Young Mania Rating Scale [YMRS] ≤7), state with manic/mixed symptoms (MS/MX; YMRS ≥8), or euthymic state (ES; HAMD-17 ≤7, YMRS ≤7). Seven classification tasks included BP vs HC, each mood state vs HC, and interstate comparisons. Feature importance was validated via permutation testing (P<.05). Medication sensitivity analyses were performed. The model achieved high discrimination for BP vs HC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]=0.916, 95% CI 0.854-0.958; sensitivity 0.933; specificity 0.859) and strong performance for mood states vs HC (AUC=0.805-0.874). Acoustic features comprised 96% to 98% of the features achieving statistical significance (P<.05), including mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, spectral characteristics, and voice quality measures, showing strong correlations with diagnostic probabilities (|ρ|=0.35-0.85) and symptom severity (HAMD-17: ρ=-0.51; YMRS: ρ=-0.37); 2 to 4 linguistic features per comparison also reached significance. With sample independence ensured for interstate comparisons, DS vs ES significantly exceeded chance (AUC=0.760, permutation P=.03), whereas MS/MX vs ES (AUC=0.601, P=.20) and DS vs MS/MX (AUC=0.569, P=.30) did not, suggesting that markers primarily reflect persistent disease characteristics with partial state-associated components in depressive states. The combined acoustic-linguistic model, driven primarily by acoustic features, shows potential as an objective aid for BP diagnosis (AUC>0.9), largely free of medication confounding; some features remained detectable during euthymia, although ES discrimination could not be fully separated from concurrent antipsychotic treatment. Although DS showed partial distinguishability from ES, overall limitations remain for monitoring mood state changes. Findings require validation in diverse populations and against other psychiatric conditions.

papers.title: Electrodiagnostic Classification of Sensory Neuropathies: Severity Clusters and Clinical Correlates.
papers.abstract: Grading sensory neuropathy severity on nerve conduction studies (NCS) is operator dependent, which limits comparisons across patients, laboratories, and studies. We aimed to develop an objective severity classification to standardize NCS reporting and support clinical decision-making. We retrospectively analyzed NCS performed at IRCCS San Raffaele Hospital (2018-2024), extracted with a validated parser. Adult studies with sensory involvement were selected using sural sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitude thresholds after excluding motor abnormalities. Hierarchical clustering combined normalized sural and "best" upper-limb (UL) SNAP amplitudes with binary indicators for absent responses. Classes were ordered by an NCS severity index and validated against clinical scales. Among 15,744 consecutive examinations, 308 met inclusion criteria. Three well-separated NCS severity classes emerged: mild (reduced but present sural and present UL SNAPs), moderate (absent sural, present UL SNAPs), and severe (absent sural and UL SNAPs). Clinical severity increased monotonically across classes. Patients in the severe class had younger age at symptom onset than those in mild-moderate classes and were more disabled (modified Rankin scale ≥ 2: 50.0% in severe vs 30.4% in moderate vs 16.2% in mild). The severe class was enriched in immune/paraneoplastic (12.5%) and genetic (40.6%) causes. By stratifying patients based on SNAP amplitudes, we identified a differential etiologic enrichment rather than a continuum of disease progression. Severe electrophysiology with motor sparing should prompt RFC1 testing and immune/paraneoplastic work-up, whereas mild to moderate abnormalities should lead to assessment for diabetes and toxic or nutritional exposures.

papers.title: Neural correlates of perceptual biases in duration perception.
papers.abstract: How we perceive a current event depends not only on its immediate context, but also on how our internal expectations are shaped by prior experience. In time perception, these expectations manifest as systematic biases, namely sequential dependence, where the current percept is influenced by the previous stimulus, and central tendency, the overestimation of short durations and underestimation of long ones. Both perceptual biases, corresponding to individual beliefs about stimulus generation, can vary substantially between participants. However, the neural responses related to inter-individual differences in these biases remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate this question in a duration reproduction task. Our EEG results show that in the frontocentral region, the Contingent Negative Variation (CNV) while experiencing the current stimulus depends on the previous stimulus regardless of sequential dependence. In contrast, in the right parietal region, the slow potential was not influenced by previous duration but associated with inter-individual differences in sequential dependence. Stimulus-offset evoked P2 amplitude was associated with both central tendency and sequential dependence and P2 amplitude varied with previous stimulus duration depending on individual sequential dependence. A Bayesian model of time perception reproduced the observed neural dynamics of the frontocentral CNV and its dependence on previous stimulus duration, suggesting that individual internal time estimates and expectations of stimulus offset are reflected in EEG responses. Our results demonstrate that both forms of perceptual bias are reflected in neural activity while experiencing the ongoing stimulus, suggesting that neural processes related to perceptual biases directly affect the measurement of time.

papers.title: Objective motion-based performance assessment in STA-MCA microanastomosis: a postprocedural debriefing platform.
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to develop and demonstrate a postprocedural motion analysis platform capable of objectively quantifying intraoperative surgeon micromovements to facilitate evidence-based self-debriefing in suturing superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery microanastomosis. The authors analyzed microscope-recorded microanastomoses performed by a cerebrovascular neurosurgeon. Seven suture-placement clips were extracted from operative videos. A computer vision tracking pipeline was implemented in Python using OpenCV to track the needle holder position across the video clips. Four motion metrics were computed for each video clip: absolute error, velocity, acceleration, and jerk. A unified reference distribution was constructed from all clips, and 95th percentile thresholds were defined for each metric. The metrics were displayed as dynamic synchronized plots alongside the corresponding video. Spectral decomposition of the position signal was performed to generate time-frequency representations, and average power in the 6- to 8-Hz band was computed as a quantitative tremor measure. To demonstrate reliable longitudinal performance tracking, the authors applied their platform to 8 recorded procedures between 2023 and 2026 and plotted the mean jerk per suture over time. Reliable tracking was achieved across 92.09% of analyzed footage. Two-dimensional trajectories were reconstructed for a total of 13,183 analyzed frames encompassing 219.82 seconds of suture-placement video (7 clips). Jerk analysis revealed multiple segments exceeding the 95th percentile threshold, flagging moments for surgical review. Time-frequency analysis revealed transient broadband power bursts and 2 persistent spectral bands (6-8 Hz and < 4 Hz). Tremor intensity analysis in the 6- to 8-Hz range revealed temporal tremor fluctuations, a finding undetectable by other metrics. Longitudinal performance tracking was feasible and demonstrated a stable jerk profile, consistent with expert-level performance. A motion-based postprocedural debriefing platform for the performance of microanastomosis is technically feasible and capable of generating objective, quantitative performance metrics from standard operative video. Unlike prior work focused on expert-novice differentiation, this platform was designed to support individualized self-assessment and reflective practice for surgeons at any experience level. Future work should validate the platform prospectively and correlate motion-based metrics with clinical outcomes.

The platform flagged jerk segments above 95th-percentile thresholds and detected temporal tremor fluctuations, demonstrating feasibility of objective motion-based postprocedural self-debriefing and longitudinal performance tracking.

papers.title: Neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants evaluated for but not treated with therapeutic hypothermia: a prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Therapeutic hypothermia (TH) is the standard of care for moderate to severe neonatal encephalopathy (NE). Although some centers consider TH for mild NE, neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants who do not meet eligibility criteria are incompletely defined. Infants evaluated for TH based on perinatal risk factors, but who did not meet institutional eligibility criteria, were prospectively enrolled. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were assessed at 24 months. Bayley-4 scores <85 were classified as sub-normative performance. Of 39 infants enrolled, 26 completed Bayley-4 assessments. Thirteen (50%) demonstrated sub-normative performance in at least one developmental domain; only one of them had an acute brain injury on MRI. Compared with infants with average-range performance, those with sub-normative performance had higher postnatal base deficits (10.1 vs 6 mmol/L, p 0.04), higher postnatal lactate levels (9.4 vs 4.9 mmol/L, p 0.05), and a trend toward less sleep-wake cycling on aEEG (45% vs 83%, p 0.06). A substantial proportion of infants evaluated for but not treated with TH demonstrated sub-normative developmental performance at 2 years. Absence of acute MRI-detected injury does not preclude later developmental vulnerability. These findings support longitudinal follow-up of infants who are evaluated for TH but do not meet TH criteria. Infants evaluated for but not treated with therapeutic hypothermia demonstrated a measurable risk of neurodevelopmental vulnerability at 2 years, with 50% demonstrating sub-normative performance (>1 SD below the normative mean) in at least one domain on the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development Fourth Edition. Early postnatal metabolic abnormalities in infants evaluated for therapeutic hypothermia showed a potential association with later developmental outcomes. There is a need for improved risk stratification and structured longitudinal follow-up for infants evaluated for but who do not meet cooling criteria.

papers.title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

papers.title: Role of reverse remodelling in recurrence of atrial fibrillation after patient-tailored catheter ablation.
papers.abstract: Catheter ablation (CA) is a curative treatment for atrial fibrillation (AF), yet success rates remain sub-optimal, with ∼50% of patients with persistent AF experiencing recurrence after 1 year. This may be due to the self-perpetuating nature of AF, which remodels atrial structure and cellular properties, while successful treatment can induce reverse remodelling (RR). This study develops a patient-specific CA strategy to directly target re-entrant drivers (RDs) and investigates the role of RR in AF recurrence. Left atrial (LA) models were reconstructed from LGE-MRI scans of AF patients (n = 15) and coupled with the Courtemanche-Ramirez-Nattel (CRN) electrophysiology model. RDs were induced via pacing, identified using DGM analysis, and targeted ablation was performed in-silico. Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) was applied as a reference. Following termination, AF recurrence was tested under three levels of electrical reverse remodelling (ERR: 0%, 50%, and 100%), with and without structural reverse remodelling (SRR). Targeted ablation acutely terminated AF in all patient-specific models. After the first procedure, AF recurrence decreased progressively from 55% at 0% ERR to 36.7% at 50% ERR and 5% at 100% ERR; with additional SRR, recurrence was further reduced to 46.7%, 26.7%, and 0%, respectively. After the second CA procedure, AF recurrence rate was 42.9%, 17.9%, and 0% without SRR and 25%, 14.3%, and 0% with SRR. This study highlights the importance of RR for therapy success, with a novel targeted CA technique ensuring <5% AF recurrence in patient-specific simulations. After clinical validation, this approach can help improve long-term patient outcomes.

papers.title: Atypical Pediatric Epilepsy: A Narrative Review of Classification, Diagnosis, and Emerging Therapeutics.
papers.abstract: Atypical pediatric epilepsies represent a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by uncommon etiologies, variable clinical presentations, and frequent resistance to standard antiseizure medications. Recent advances in classification, along with developments in genomics, neuroimaging, and autoimmune neurology, have expanded the recognized spectrum of these conditions. However, a significant proportion of children remain without a definitive syndromic diagnosis, underscoring ongoing limitations in current frameworks. This review provides a comprehensive overview of atypical epilepsy in children, including evolving classification systems, epidemiology, and etiological mechanisms spanning genetic, structural, metabolic, and immune-mediated causes. Key syndromes - including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome, infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, and febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome - are discussed with emphasis on clinical features, differential diagnosis, and prognosis. Diagnostic challenges such as phenotypic overlap, EEG limitations, and barriers to timely genetic testing are also examined. Emerging therapeutic strategies highlight a paradigm shift from broad-spectrum seizure control toward precision medicine, including targeted pharmacologic agents, antisense oligonucleotides, gene therapies, and neuromodulation approaches. Improved recognition and classification of atypical epilepsies, coupled with early implementation of targeted therapies, are essential to optimize outcomes in this vulnerable population.

papers.title: Restitution properties during ventricular fibrillation and the effects of cardiac pacing location on ventricular electrophysiology in the rabbit heart.
papers.abstract: Sudden cardiac death is a cause of mortality due to malignant arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation (VF). Although action potential duration (APD) restitution is a method to assess arrhythmic susceptibility, repolarisation may depend on prior activation history, a phenomenon known as cardiac memory. Cardiac memory describes the persistence of repolarisation effects from previous beats, such that APD reflects not only the immediately preceding diastolic interval (DI) but also earlier activation effects. This may be relevant during VF, where continuously varying activation patterns prevent a steady electrophysiological state. This study investigated how pacing location affects ventricular electrophysiology and whether repolarisation during VF exhibits short-term cardiac memory. Langendorff-perfused rabbit hearts were used to record monophasic action potentials from the left ventricular apex and base. Pacing was conducted from five sites. Steady-state APD was assessed during constant pacing. Effective refractory period (ERP), APD restitution and conduction time restitution (CTR) were assessed using an S1-S2 extra-stimulus protocol (S1, conditioning stimuli; S2, premature extra-stimulus). Additionally, APD-DI and APD-APD relationships were analysed during early VF. Pacing location significantly influenced S1 and S2 conduction delays, consistent with site-dependent activation timing. However, steady-state APD, ERP and CTR were not significantly affected by pacing location. In contrast, during VF, APD exhibited a significant dependence on preceding DI and preceding APD over approximately the first 30 beats, with these relationships progressively deteriorating thereafter. These findings demonstrate that while pacing location alters activation timing, repolarisation dynamics under stable activation histories are robust. During VF, continuously changing activation patterns unmask short-term cardiac memory.

papers.title: Atypical Atrial Flutter From Lipomatous Hypertrophy of the Interatrial Septum in a Procedure-Naive Patient.
papers.abstract: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum (LHIS) is generally benign and often discovered incidentally; however, it can occasionally serve as a substrate for atrial arrhythmias. An 86-year-old man with no prior cardiac history presented with new onset atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial rate of 280 beats/min. During an electrophysiology study, intracardiac echocardiography identified LHIS. Three-dimensional electroanatomic activation mapping demonstrated the earliest focal activation at the superior posteroseptal right atrium, corresponding to the location of the LHIS. Radiofrequency ablation at this site terminated the AFL, rendering the tachycardia noninducible. LHIS can act as an isolated arrhythmogenic substrate for atypical AFL. The combination of intracardiac echocardiography and high-density electroanatomic mapping allows precise localization of the arrhythmogenic focus, facilitating safe and effective catheter ablation. LHIS should be considered a potential arrhythmogenic substrate in patients with atypical AFL. Catheter ablation of LHIS-associated AFL is safe and effective.

papers.title: Reported Life-Threatening Polymorphic Ventricular Arrhythmia With Torsade-Like Morphology in a Patient With Gordon Syndrome and Hyperkalaemia.
papers.abstract: Gordon's syndrome (pseudohypoaldosteronism type II) is a rare, inherited tubulopathy characterised by salt-sensitive hypertension, hyperkalaemia, and metabolic acidosis despite preserved renal function. Pathogenic variants affecting the with-no-lysine (K) signalling pathway include WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, and CUL3. We report the case of a 37-year-old woman with genetically confirmed CUL3-related Gordon's syndrome who developed hyperkalaemia after a three-week interruption of bendroflumethiazide. During pre-hospital assessment, ambulance clinicians documented a self-terminating rhythm that they identified as torsade de pointes. The original recording cannot be retrieved; consequently, the rhythm classification, preceding QT interval, and possible alternative rhythm or artefact could not be independently assessed. Point-of-care venous blood gas potassium was 4.8 mmol/L, whereas formal laboratory potassium was 6.1 mmol/L. The sampling and processing information available did not establish the cause of this discrepancy. Subsequent echocardiography, computed tomography coronary angiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing, and additional electrical assessment did not identify a definitive alternative substrate, although an intermittent electrical disorder could not be excluded. Following treatment of hyperkalaemia and multidisciplinary cardiology and electrophysiology review, an extravascular implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. Bendroflumethiazide was resumed, with subsequent improvement in potassium control. This case highlights the importance of uninterrupted thiazide therapy in Gordon's syndrome, assessment of discordant potassium measurements, and careful interpretation of a reported serious rhythm event when its original tracing is unavailable. The temporal association with hyperkalaemia does not establish that it caused torsade de pointes.
